findings.title: Denial cache key omits identity type
findings.body: Check builds the denial cache key from namespace, UserUID, action, name, and parent folder only, without including the identity type. validateSubject permits multiple identity types, and anonymous:0 and render:0 both parse to UserUID 0. A denied anonymous check can therefore write a denial cache entry that a later render:0 check hits, causing the renderer to be denied before getRendererPermissions can allow read access. The denial key must be scoped by identity type.

findings.title: Unescaped underscore-separated denial cache keys can collide
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, user UID, action, resource name, and parent folder with underscores and no escaping. If a resource or folder UID contains an underscore, different (name, parent) pairs can produce the same key; for example, name a_b with parent c collides with name a and parent b_c. Because this key stores authorization denials, a collision can cause a denial recorded for one resource/folder combination to be applied to a different resource, incorrectly denying access.

findings.title: Negative denial cache can mask newly granted permissions
findings.body: Check consults the denial cache before the newly added DB fallback and writes a denial entry whenever a permission check fails. The denial entry is not invalidated when permissions or folder relationships change. If the initial denial is caused by stale permissions, replica lag, or a stale folder tree cache, the denial entry continues to block subsequent checks until its TTL expires, even if a fresh database lookup would now allow access. This can delay access to newly created dashboards or folders and counteracts the fallback behavior added by this PR.

findings.title: Denial-cache test does not prove the denial entry overrides permissions
findings.body: The test sets the positive permission cache entry to {"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. In checkPermission, only true scope-map entries grant access, so this cached value does not allow the request even if the denial cache is ignored. The test would still pass without the denial-cache lookup. To verify the denial cache, cache a true permission (or database permissions) and assert that the explicit denial entry still causes denial.
